displayQuote: A wise man proportions his belief to the evidence

meta.title: Who really said "A wise man proportions his belief to the evidence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, David Hume wrote it — in "Of Miracles," An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748). The original adds one word: "therefore."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A wise man proportions his belief to the evidence'?
meta.ogDescription: A genuine David Hume line from 1748's Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X 'Of Miracles.' The original reads 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Hume wrote this in Section X (“Of Miracles”), Part I of An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, first published in 1748 as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding. The original reads “A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence” — the popular version simply drops the connective “therefore.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Section X, “Of Miracles,” Part I (para. E 10.4)

source.excerpt: A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence. In such conclusions as are founded on an infallible experience, he expects the event with the last degree of assurance, and regards his past experience as a full proof of the future existence of that event.
trail: The primary text is on davidhume.org, the scholarly Hume Texts Online edition ↗, which places the line at Section X, Part I, para. E 10.4.
Quote Investigator ↗ dates the sentence to Hume’s 1748 essay and quotes it as “A wise Man, therefore, proportions his Belief to the Evidence.”
A public-domain full text of the chapter is mirrored at ourcivilisation.com ↗ for the surrounding context.
source.excerptNote: The sentence opens Hume’s argument in “Of Miracles” that testimony for a miracle must be weighed against the uniform experience that argues against it.

author.name: David Hume
author.heading: About David Hume
author.bio: David Hume was a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, best known for a rigorous empiricism that grounded all knowledge in experience. His An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) reworked the ideas of his earlier Treatise of Human Nature into a more accessible form, and its Section X, “Of Miracles,” remains one of philosophy’s most cited arguments about the weighing of testimony and evidence.

misattribution.heading: One word gets dropped
misattribution.intro: This line is genuinely Hume’s — the only real distortion is a small one of wording, plus a broader idea often blurred into it.

items.why: Hume’s original reads “A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.” The circulating version drops the connective “therefore,” which linked the sentence to the reasoning that precedes it in the Enquiry ↗.
That more famous slogan is often credited to Hume, but as Quote Investigator ↗ documents, its modern phrasing traces to Marcello Truzzi and Carl Sagan in the 1970s–80s, not to Hume himself.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is sound: Hume wrote this in Section X of the 1748 Enquiry ↗ — just with a “therefore” the internet tends to leave out.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The sentence is the hinge of Hume’s celebrated essay “Of Miracles.” Having argued that belief in any matter of fact rests on experience, Hume concludes that a rational person weighs each claim in proportion to the evidence supporting it — and that the uniform experience against a miracle is itself a “proof” that testimony must overcome.
The principle became a cornerstone of empiricist epistemology and, later, of scientific skepticism, echoing in probability theory and in modern debates over extraordinary claims.
context.pull: In proportion as the fact is more or less unusual, the evidence must be weighed more or less heavily.
